title: Split a loaf cake into two layers with a wire
instruction: Split the loaf cake into two layers of equal height with the cutting wire. Pick up the wire by its two handles, hold it taut and draw it level through the cake along its length, half way up: 30 mm above the mat the cake stands on, where its sides are scored. Do not touch the cake with the grippers. Leave the cake where it is with the top layer still lying on the bottom one, and put the wire down on the table when you have finished.
context: A cake-cutting wire must stay taut and level to split a loaf into even layers. Both hands control the wire while the cake is held in place only by friction on the mat.
setup: Units mm. x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y left (+) or right (-) of the midline, z up from the table top. Two YAM arms with parallel grippers (pads 94 apart when open), bases at (0, +305) and (0, -305), start at their ready pose with grippers open; one overhead camera and one camera on each wrist. Table top: wood, 1100 x 1300; nothing else is on it. 0) Work surface: matt black self-adhesive vinyl film (0.1 thick), 540 (x) x 600 (y), stuck flat to the table from x = 60 to 600 and y = -300 to +300, so that the pale handles and the wire show against it. 1) Stand: a dark wooden chopping block 250 (x) x 150 (y) x 40 tall, centred at (400, 0), standing on the film and fixed to the table with double-sided tape; a black silicone baking mat cut to 246 x 146 is laid on its top (under 1 thick), so that a rim of wood shows round it. 2) Cake: an Entenmann's All Butter Loaf Cake, 11.5 oz (326 g), sold boxed in US supermarkets, taken out of its box and paper tray, at room temperature and within its date; about 185 long x 90 wide x 60 tall. It stands on the mat with its length along x, centred at (400, 0); chalk marks on the mat show its corners. It looks like any loaf baked in a paper tray: golden brown on top, where it has risen to a ridge and split open along the middle, paler golden on the sides and ends, rounded at the corners. A line is scored with a knife, about 1 wide and 1 deep, along both long sides and both ends, 30 above the mat (70 above the table), the way bakers mark a cake before they split it with a wire or a thread; it shows as a fine pale line in the golden side, not as a gap. 3) Cutting wire: a Fante's Uncle Paolo's Cheese Wire, 12 in (model 2552), which its maker also sells for cutting cakes into layers: 305 of fine stainless steel wire, about 0.5 thick, with a wooden handle at each end, each about 65 long, 12 thick and 5 g. The handles lie flat on the table pointing away from the robot, their middles at (140, +130) and (140, -130); the wire lies slack on the table between them, bowed away from the robot as far as x = 204. The cake lets the wire through its 90 width at a steady pull of about 1.4 N in all and starts to slide on the mat at about 3 N; both can be checked with a 5 N spring scale (see README). The cake's size, its cutting resistance and friction, and the handles' size and mass and the wire's thickness are estimates, not published figures. What the policy's cameras (320 x 176 pixels) show, by projection into their calibrated positions: the overhead camera shows each handle as a pale stroke about 2 x 13 pixels on the black film, the cake's top as a golden-brown bar about 17 x 29 pixels on the black mat, with the paler split 1 to 2 pixels wide along its middle, the cake's near end about 5 pixels tall and the wooden front of the stand about 3, and the wire as a light line about one pixel wide because it is drawn 5 thick (at its real thickness it would cover a tenth of a pixel). It cannot see the cake's long sides, and the scored line on the near end is far below a pixel, which is why the instruction gives the height. A gripper lowered over a handle sees it 16 to 28 pixels across and the wire 7 to 11. At the start each wrist camera has only the far end of the cake's side, at the edge of its image; one brought 120 to 200 from the cake's side shows the score 1 to 2 pixels wide. The layout is the same in every trial.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial from a photo from above, a ruler and the trial video. (a) Cut length: how far the cut runs along each of the cake's two long sides within 5 mm of the scored line. (b) Cut through: the top layer is cut free over its whole area; it lifts off whole, and both layers are 25 to 35 mm thick at the four corners and at the middle of each long side, measured with a ruler against the cut faces (in simulation, 99 percent of the cake's plan is cut within 5 mm of the line). (c) Spoiled: more than 5 percent of the cake's plan (8 cm2) is cut anywhere else: a second cut, or a cut that wanders more than 5 mm from the line; in a real trial also a layer torn or broken into pieces. (d) Touched: at any time a gripper or arm touched the cake (in simulation, pressed on it with more than 0.05 N). (e) In place: the cake is within 10 mm and 5 degrees of its chalk marks and the top layer still lies on the bottom one, within 10 mm and 5 degrees of where it was cut. (f) Put down: throughout the last 2 s both handles lie on the table top (not on the stand or the cake), both grippers are open, each gripper's centre point (midway between its fingertips) is at least 5 cm from both handles and from the cake, and nothing moves. Score 0 if the cut runs less than 60 mm along either long side, or if the cake was touched. Otherwise: 0.25 if the cake is not cut through or is spoiled; 0.5 if it is cut through and not spoiled; 0.75 if, in addition, cake and top layer are in place; 1.0 if, in addition, the wire is put down. Which way the wire is drawn and which arm does what do not matter. The trial ends at the run limit, or as soon as 1.0 is reached. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.
reset_notes: One cake per trial (about 5 to 6 US dollars); a cut cake cannot be used again, because a second cut at the same height meets no crumb. Take the cut cake away, brush the crumbs off the mat and the film, take a fresh cake out of its box and tray, stand it on the chalk marks and score the line 30 mm above the mat along its sides and ends with a knife held flat on a 30 mm block (2 minutes). Use cakes of one batch where possible and weigh each one; they vary by a few grams and millimetres. Food hygiene: only the wire touches the cake, and the grippers touch only the wooden handles; wash the wire between trials and do not eat the cakes. If a failed trial put a gripper into the cake, wipe the finger pads clean of crumbs and butter before the next trial (thin disposable finger covers make this quicker). Lay the wire out with the handles on their marks. Arms at their ready pose, grippers open. In simulation: seed 0, zero object jitter; both layers and both handles are returned to their authored poses with zero velocity, the record of the cut is cleared, the wire is laid slack between the handles, and the scorer starts fresh.
fidelity: PhysX rigid cake layers; a cut-response rule uses a 2.5 mm grid, not fracture physics. The wire is 64 massless stretch springs, capped at 40 N; drawn 5 mm thick, physically 0.5 mm. Wire/link contact does not feed force to arms; loose-handle coupling is reduced for stability. No cake compression, crumbling or tearing. Dimensions, cutting resistance and friction are estimates; no hardware trial. Full details: REFERENCE-SPEC.json and TECHNICAL.md.
